This baby may have birth asphyxia with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, but other urgent causes such as neonatal sepsis, low blood sugar, low calcium, maternal sedative/opioid drugs, prematurity, or birth injury must also be considered.

Immediate action is neonatal resuscitation: keep the baby warm, position and clear the airway if needed, stimulate, give bag-mask ventilation if not breathing well, add oxygen, and start chest compressions if the heart rate remains below 60/min despite good ventilation.  
Give IV dextrose if hypoglycaemia is present, treat seizures promptly, start antibiotics if infection is suspected, and avoid oral feeding until the baby is stable; use expressed breast milk by tube later if needed.  
The baby should be urgently managed in a newborn unit/NICU, and if moderate or severe birth asphyxia is confirmed within 6 hours, therapeutic cooling should be considered where safely available.

A bite from an unvaccinated dog can transmit rabies, which is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so start post-exposure prophylaxis immediately—do not wait to see if the dog becomes sick.

He should also receive tetanus protection as appropriate, pain relief, and antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate because redness and swelling may mean early bacterial infection; the wound should be examined for depth, foreign material, tendon/nerve injury, and usually should not be tightly stitched unless necessary.

Tests are usually not needed for rabies prevention, but the clinician may request wound culture, full blood count, or X-ray if there is pus, fever, severe swelling, crush injury, or concern for bone involvement.

Blue or dusky lips in a newborn usually mean low oxygen in the blood (cyanosis), and difficulty breathing or stopping feeds during breastfeeding is a serious danger sign requiring urgent hospital assessment.  
Possible causes include congenital heart disease, severe infection/pneumonia or sepsis, aspiration/choking during feeds, airway problems, prematurity-related breathing problems, or low blood sugar; liver disease usually causes yellow eyes/skin (jaundice), not blue lips.  
Other danger signs are fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, pauses in breathing, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness or limpness, fever or low temperature, convulsions, persistent vomiting, severe jaundice, or reduced urine.  
While going to hospital, stop feeding if she becomes breathless or blue, keep her warm, place her on her side or upright with the head slightly extended, and gently clear visible mucus—do not force feeds or give home medicines.  
Emergency treatment should be given by health workers and may include oxygen, checking blood sugar with glucose if low, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and referral for heart/oxygen testing such as pulse oximetry and echocardiography.

A child with severe night cough, wheezing and difficulty breathing may have asthma or viral-induced wheeze, but pneumonia, whooping cough, tuberculosis, allergy, or an inhaled foreign body can also cause similar symptoms.  
Night-time cough with a “whistling” chest often happens because the airways become narrowed and inflamed, so the child should be assessed at a clinic for oxygen level, chest examination, and treatment such as inhaled salbutamol with a spacer if indicated.  
Danger signs include fast breathing, chest indrawing, bluish lips, inability to talk/cry/feed, severe weakness or drowsiness, persistent high fever, noisy breathing at rest, vomiting everything, convulsions, coughing blood, or symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks.  
Avoid smoke from cigarettes, firewood/charcoal or kerosene, dust, strong perfumes/insecticides, mould, cold air exposure, and known allergy triggers.

This woman should be treated as suspected severe pre-eclampsia because headache, visual symptoms, facial/limb swelling and BP around 168/100 in pregnancy are danger signs, even if the BP later falls.  
She needs urgent hospital/obstetric review: repeat BP correctly, check urine protein, full blood count/platelets, kidney and liver tests, monitor urine output and baby’s wellbeing, and admit or refer to a facility able to manage emergencies.  
To prevent eclampsia, give magnesium sulphate when severe features are present, control BP with pregnancy-safe drugs such as labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine, and plan delivery when indicated because delivery is the definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia.  
She should avoid self-medication such as analgesic powders/NSAIDs unless prescribed, and return immediately for worsening headache, blurred vision, fits, chest pain, breathlessness, reduced urine, severe abdominal pain, or reduced fetal movement.  
Prevention includes early and regular antenatal care with BP and urine checks, taking prescribed medicines, low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks and calcium supplementation for women at risk or with low calcium intake, and prompt reporting of danger signs rather than waiting at home.

Yes, this may be grief after losing his mother, but because he is withdrawing, not eating, and appears persistently sad, he should be assessed for depression, traumatic grief, and any risk of self-harm.

Not every breast lump is cancer, especially in younger women, but no woman should assume it is harmless without proper assessment.  
She should attend a clinic or hospital for “triple assessment”: breast examination by a clinician, imaging such as ultrasound or mammogram depending on age, and a needle test/biopsy if needed.  
Warning signs include a lump that is hard, growing or fixed, nipple discharge especially blood, nipple turning inward, skin dimpling or thickening like orange peel, breast ulcer, redness/swelling, change in breast size or shape, or lumps in the armpit.  
She should avoid massaging, applying herbs, or delaying care, because early diagnosis greatly improves treatment outcomes if it is cancer.

A 7-day-old baby with blocked/noisy breathing and poor breastfeeding should be taken to a hospital or neonatal clinic urgently today, because poor feeding and breathing difficulty are danger signs in newborns.

The child is most likely having a febrile convulsion, a seizure triggered by high fever, but serious causes such as malaria, meningitis, or severe infection must be ruled out urgently.  
Lay the child on the side, remove dangerous objects, loosen tight clothing, and do not put anything in the mouth or try to force-feed during the seizure.

Reduce the fever with tepid sponging and paracetamol if the child can swallow safely, but avoid cold baths or overdosing.

His symptoms—excessive thirst, passing large volumes of urine day and night, tiredness and blurred vision—strongly suggest diabetes mellitus, because high blood sugar pulls water into the urine causing dehydration, thirst, fatigue and visual changes.

Danger signs include talk of death or suicide, self-harm, giving away belongings, severe hopelessness, hearing voices, extreme agitation, violence, not eating/drinking, substance misuse, abuse, or sudden major behaviour change—these need urgent medical help immediately.  
It is appropriate for her to see a trained counsellor, psychologist, psychiatric nurse, doctor, or mental health specialist, especially if symptoms last more than two weeks, affect school/work/home life, or are worsening.  
A health worker can assess her safely, check for physical causes, provide counselling, involve family support, and arrange treatment if depression or anxiety is confirmed.

Heavy vaginal bleeding 6 weeks after the last period must be treated as an emergency and pregnancy-related causes must be ruled out first: threatened/incomplete miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy; other causes include fibroids, adenomyosis, polyps, pelvic infection, bleeding disorders, hormonal anovulation, and rarely cancer.  
Immediate steps are ABC assessment, vital signs, two large-bore IV lines, oxygen if needed, IV normal saline/Ringer’s lactate, urinary catheter, urgent blood grouping/cross-match and transfusion if shocked or severely anaemic, while calling a gynaecology/surgical team.

If bleeding continues or retained products/ectopic pregnancy are found, she may need manual vacuum aspiration/D&C, uterine balloon tamponade, laparoscopy/laparotomy, or other surgery.  
Key tests are urgent urine/serum pregnancy test or beta-hCG, full blood count, blood group and cross-match, clotting profile, pelvic ultrasound, malaria test where relevant, renal/liver tests, thyroid test if recurrent, STI testing, and later Pap smear or endometrial biopsy if age/risk factors suggest cancer.

Severe lower abdominal pain with heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is an obstetric emergency and can be caused by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy (early pregnancy), placental abruption, placenta previa, preterm labour, infection, or rarely uterine rupture.
